stem: A mixture of benzoic acid and naphthalene in diethyl ether is shaken with aqueous NaOH. Which species ends up mainly in the aqueous layer?
explanation: Correct: C) NaOH deprotonates benzoic acid to the ionic, water-soluble sodium benzoate, which partitions into the aqueous layer while naphthalene stays in the ether. Why the others are wrong: A) Naphthalene is nonpolar and neutral, so it remains in the ether. B) Benzoic acid is protonated and neutral only without base; with NaOH it is converted to its salt. D) Diethyl ether is the organic solvent, not a solute in the aqueous layer.
trap: Forgetting that ionization makes an organic acid water soluble.

stem: Which aqueous wash would best remove an amine impurity from an organic layer?
explanation: Correct: D) Dilute HCl protonates the amine to a water-soluble ammonium salt that moves into the aqueous layer. Why the others are wrong: A) Dilute NaOH keeps the amine neutral, so it stays in the organic layer. B) Brine alone does not ionize the amine, so it stays organic. C) Pure water does not protonate the amine, so little is removed.
trap: Using base to extract a basic compound.

stem: Dichloromethane (density 1.33 g/mL) is shaken with water in a separatory funnel. Where is the organic layer?
explanation: Correct: A) The denser liquid sits at the bottom; dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL) is denser than water and immiscible with it, so it forms the bottom layer. Why the others are wrong: B) Top would apply to a less dense solvent like diethyl ether. C) A single layer would require miscibility, but DCM and water are immiscible. D) The stopcock is a valve, not a layer location.
trap: Assuming organic layers are always on top.

stem: Two miscible liquids have boiling points of 80 C and 90 C. Which technique is best to separate them?
explanation: Correct: B) A fractionating column provides many vaporization-condensation cycles, needed when boiling points differ by only about 10 C. Why the others are wrong: A) Simple distillation works only if the difference is large (about 25 C or more). C) Filtration separates solids from liquids, not miscible liquids. D) Recrystallization purifies solids, not liquid mixtures.
trap: Choosing simple distillation for close boiling points.

stem: Vacuum distillation is used for compounds that:

options.C: Have very high boiling points or decompose when heated

explanation: Correct: C) Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so high-boiling or heat-sensitive compounds distill without decomposing. Why the others are wrong: A) Compounds boiling below room temperature do not need vacuum. B) Solids are purified by other methods such as recrystallization. D) Water immiscibility is irrelevant to vacuum distillation.
trap: Thinking vacuum raises boiling point.

stem: Fractional distillation of an ethanol-water mixture cannot produce pure ethanol because:

options.C: Water has a lower boiling point than ethanol
options.D: A minimum-boiling azeotrope forms near 95% ethanol

explanation: Correct: D) A minimum-boiling azeotrope forms near 95% ethanol, where vapor and liquid have the same composition, so further enrichment is impossible. Why the others are wrong: A) Ethanol and water are fully miscible. B) Ethanol does not decompose at its boiling point. C) Water boils higher (100 C) than ethanol (78 C), not lower.
trap: Assuming distillation can separate any mixture of liquids.

stem: The ideal recrystallization solvent dissolves the compound:

options.A: Well when hot and poorly when cold
options.D: Poorly when hot and well when cold

explanation: Correct: A) The compound dissolves when hot and crystallizes when cold, leaving soluble impurities in the mother liquor. Why the others are wrong: B) Dissolving well at all temperatures gives no crystals on cooling. C) Dissolving poorly at all temperatures never dissolves the compound. D) This reverses the temperature dependence and would precipitate on heating.
trap: Reversing the temperature dependence.

stem: Slow cooling during recrystallization generally yields:

options.A: Smaller crystals with more impurities trapped
options.D: Lower purity because crystals grow too slowly

explanation: Correct: B) Slow growth lets the crystal lattice exclude foreign molecules, giving larger, purer crystals. Why the others are wrong: A) Smaller crystals with trapped impurities result from rapid cooling. C) Slow cooling gives crystals, not an amorphous liquid. D) Slow cooling improves purity, not lowers it.
trap: Believing fast cooling is better.

stem: In TLC, a compound spot travels 2.4 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. What is the Rf?
explanation: Correct: C) Rf = distance by compound / distance by solvent front = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30. Why the others are wrong: A) 3.3 inverts the ratio (8.0/2.4). B) 0.70 is 1 - 0.30, the fraction of the front not travelled. D) 0.19 has no basis in the data.
trap: Inverting the ratio and reporting solvent-front over spot distance instead of spot over front.

stem: On a silica gel TLC plate, which compound will generally have the lowest Rf?
explanation: Correct: D) Polar compounds adsorb more strongly to polar silica and move less, giving the lowest Rf. Why the others are wrong: A) The least polar compound travels farthest, giving the highest Rf. B) Size alone is not the determinant of Rf on silica. C) Volatility is not the determinant of Rf on silica.
trap: Assuming polar compounds travel farther.

stem: Increasing the polarity of the eluent in normal-phase chromatography will generally:

options.A: Increase the Rf values of the compounds

explanation: Correct: A) A more polar eluent competes with analytes for silica binding sites, moving them farther and raising Rf. Why the others are wrong: B) Decreasing Rf would require a less polar eluent. C) Eluent polarity does change Rf values. D) The stationary phase remains polar silica; it is not reversed.
trap: Thinking a more polar solvent holds compounds back.

stem: In normal-phase column chromatography on silica, which compound elutes first?

options.D: The one with the highest charge

explanation: Correct: B) Weakly adsorbed nonpolar compounds are retained least on silica, so the least polar elutes first. Why the others are wrong: A) The most polar binds silica strongly and elutes last. C) Size is not the main basis in adsorption chromatography. D) Charge is not the main basis; polar groups bind silica and slow elution.
trap: Mixing up normal and reverse phase elution order.

stem: In reverse-phase HPLC with a C18 column, which compound elutes first?

options.D: The compound with the longest alkyl chain

explanation: Correct: C) The C18 stationary phase is nonpolar; polar compounds interact least with it and elute first. Why the others are wrong: A) The most nonpolar compound interacts strongly with C18 and is retained longest. B) The largest hydrocarbon is highly nonpolar and is retained strongly. D) The longest alkyl chain is the most nonpolar and is retained strongly.
trap: Applying normal-phase rules to reverse-phase systems.

stem: In size-exclusion chromatography, which molecules elute first?
explanation: Correct: D) Large molecules cannot enter the bead pores and take the shorter path, eluting first. Why the others are wrong: A) Small molecules enter the pores and elute later. B) Charge is not the basis of separation in size exclusion. C) Hydrophobicity is not the basis of separation in size exclusion.
trap: Assuming small molecules travel fastest.

stem: A protein with pI 9.0 is applied at pH 7 to a column containing negatively charged resin (a cation exchanger). The protein will:

options.A: Bind to the column because it is positively charged
options.B: Pass through because it is positive
options.C: Bind because it is negatively charged
options.D: Pass through because it has no charge

explanation: Correct: A) At pH 7, below the pI of 9.0, the protein has a net positive charge and binds the negatively charged resin. Why the others are wrong: B) Passing through because it is positive is wrong; positive charge causes binding. C) It is positive, not negative, at pH below its pI, and negative would be repelled. D) It is not neutral at pH 7; it is neutral only at its pI of 9.0.
trap: Reversing the charge relative to pI.

stem: A protein bound to a cation-exchange column can be eluted by:

options.C: Lowering the pH below the pI

explanation: Correct: B) Increasing salt provides competing cations that displace the protein from the negatively charged resin. Why the others are wrong: A) Decreasing salt reduces competition and increases binding. C) Lowering the pH below the pI increases positive charge and binding. D) Cooling has little effect on electrostatic binding.
trap: Believing lower pH helps release a cation-bound protein.

stem: A His-tagged protein is purified on a nickel column. How is it commonly eluted?

options.C: With imidazole, which competes for nickel

explanation: Correct: C) Imidazole mimics the histidine ring and competes for nickel, displacing the His tag. Why the others are wrong: A) High pH water alone would not disrupt metal coordination effectively. B) Size cutoff is not the basis of affinity chromatography. D) Nonpolar solvents would denature the protein and do not target nickel binding.
trap: Ignoring specific competitive elution.

stem: In SDS-PAGE, proteins separate primarily by:
explanation: Correct: D) SDS denatures proteins and imparts uniform negative charge per mass, so migration depends on molecular mass. Why the others are wrong: A) Native charge is masked by SDS. B) pI-based separation requires isoelectric focusing, not SDS-PAGE. C) Hydrophobicity is masked by SDS coating and is not the separation basis.
trap: Assuming charge drives SDS-PAGE separation.

stem: In native PAGE, migration depends on:
explanation: Correct: A) Proteins remain folded and keep native charge, so migration depends on charge, size and shape. Why the others are wrong: B) Mass only describes SDS-PAGE, where charge-to-mass is uniform. C) Disulfide count alone does not determine native migration. D) Sequence alone ignores folding, charge and shape effects.
trap: Confusing native and denaturing gels.

stem: In isoelectric focusing, a protein stops migrating when:

options.A: The gel runs out of buffer
options.B: The pH equals its pI so its net charge is zero

explanation: Correct: B) Along the pH gradient the protein moves until pH equals its pI, where net charge is zero. Why the others are wrong: A) Running out of buffer is not the stopping mechanism. C) Pore size is not the basis in isoelectric focusing. D) A positively charged protein would still migrate toward the cathode.
trap: Mixing up pI with molecular weight.

stem: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate toward the:

options.A: Cathode, with larger fragments moving faster
options.B: Anode, with larger fragments moving faster
options.C: Anode (positive electrode), with smaller fragments moving faster
options.D: Cathode, with smaller fragments moving faster

explanation: Correct: C) The phosphate backbone is negatively charged so DNA moves toward the anode, and smaller fragments pass through pores more easily. Why the others are wrong: A) Cathode with larger fragments faster is wrong on both direction and size dependence. B) Anode with larger fragments faster is right on direction but reverses size dependence. D) Cathode with smaller fragments faster is wrong on direction because negative DNA does not go to the negative electrode.
trap: Forgetting that DNA is negatively charged, so it moves to the positive electrode, or reversing which fragments move faster through the gel.

stem: Which gel is best to resolve very small DNA fragments differing by a few base pairs?
explanation: Correct: D) Polyacrylamide has smaller, more uniform pores that resolve fragments differing by a few base pairs. Why the others are wrong: A) Low-percentage agarose has large pores that resolve only larger fragments. B) Paper is not an electrophoresis sieving matrix for DNA fragments. C) A starch-free medium names no sieving matrix and offers no resolving power.
trap: Using agarose for every DNA size range even when pores are too large for tiny fragments.

stem: In differential centrifugation of a cell homogenate at low speed, which pellets first?
explanation: Correct: A) Larger, denser components such as nuclei and unbroken cells sediment at the lowest g-force. Why the others are wrong: B) Ribosomes are very small and need ultracentrifugation speeds. C) Soluble enzymes remain in the supernatant at low speed. D) Small vesicles need higher speeds than nuclei to pellet.
trap: Assuming small components pellet first.

stem: In equilibrium density gradient centrifugation, particles stop at the position where:

options.B: Their density equals the gradient density

explanation: Correct: B) At equilibrium, a particle's buoyant density equals the medium density, so net force is zero and it stops. Why the others are wrong: A) Mass does not determine the final position in an equilibrium gradient. C) Particles stop at their matching density, not necessarily at the bottom. D) Charge neutrality is not the stopping criterion in centrifugation.
trap: Treating this as a velocity-based sedimentation.

stem: In gas chromatography with a nonpolar column, which compound generally elutes first?

options.A: The one with the highest boiling point
options.B: The one with the largest mass
options.C: The one with the lowest boiling point

explanation: Correct: C) More volatile, lower-boiling compounds spend more time in the mobile gas phase, so they elute first. Why the others are wrong: A) The highest-boiling compound is retained longest on the column. B) Mass alone does not set elution order; boiling point does. D) The most polar compound is retained more on a nonpolar column and elutes later.
trap: Reversing volatility so that the highest-boiling compound is assumed to elute first.

stem: Dialysis tubing is used to:

options.A: Separate large molecules from each other
options.D: Remove small solutes from a solution of large molecules

explanation: Correct: D) Small solutes diffuse across the semipermeable membrane while macromolecules remain inside the tubing. Why the others are wrong: A) Dialysis cannot separate macromolecules of similar size from each other. B) Dialysis removes small molecules rather than concentrating them. C) Dialysis separates by size cutoff, not by charge.
trap: Mistaking dialysis for chromatography.

stem: Hot filtration during recrystallization is used to:
explanation: Correct: A) Insoluble material stays on the filter while the hot product solution passes through. Why the others are wrong: B) Soluble impurities stay in solution and are removed in the cold mother liquor, not by hot filtration. C) Hot filtration is done while hot to prevent crystallization; crystallization is induced by cooling afterward. D) Drying is a separate later step.
trap: Confusing the purpose of hot filtration with cooling.

stem: Which compound mixture could be purified by sublimation?

options.A: Two liquids with similar boiling points
options.B: A solid that has a significant vapor pressure below its melting point mixed with nonvolatile impurities

explanation: Correct: B) A solid with significant vapor pressure below its melting point vaporizes and re-deposits on a cold surface, leaving nonvolatile impurities behind. Why the others are wrong: A) Two liquids of similar boiling points would need fractional distillation. C) A salt dissolved in water is separated by evaporation or crystallization, not sublimation. D) Two proteins of differing mass are separated by chromatography or electrophoresis.
trap: Assuming sublimation only applies to dry ice.

stem: To extract the most solute from water into an organic solvent using a fixed total volume of solvent, it is best to:
explanation: Correct: C) Multiple small extractions remove more solute than a single extraction using the same total solvent volume. Why the others are wrong: A) A single large portion is less efficient than several small portions. B) Pure water is the original solvent and would not extract into the organic phase. D) Heating does not improve the distribution and may evaporate the solvent.
trap: Assuming one extraction is enough.

stem: A solute has K = [ether]/[water] = 4. A 100 mL aqueous solution contains 1.0 g of solute. One extraction with 100 mL ether removes how much solute?
explanation: Correct: D) Fraction extracted = K V_o/(K V_o + V_w) = 400/(400 + 100) = 0.80, so 0.80 g is removed. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.50 g would result from K = 1. B) 0.20 g is the fraction remaining in the water, not the amount extracted. C) 4.0 g exceeds the 1.0 g total present.
trap: Ignoring volumes in an extraction calculation.

stem: In paper chromatography of amino acids, ninhydrin is used to:
explanation: Correct: A) Ninhydrin reacts with amino groups to produce a colored product, visualizing the spots. Why the others are wrong: B) It does not drive migration; the solvent does. C) It does not remove cellulose. D) It is a stain, not a charge neutralizer.
trap: Thinking ninhydrin is the mobile phase.

stem: Adding high concentrations of ammonium sulfate to a protein solution typically:

options.B: Precipitates proteins by reducing their solubility

explanation: Correct: B) High salt competes for water, reducing protein solubility and promoting aggregation (salting out), usually without denaturing. Why the others are wrong: A) Says irreversible denaturation, but proteins often remain active. C) Says solubility increases, but it decreases at high salt. D) Says peptide bonds are cut, but no hydrolysis occurs.
trap: Assuming precipitation equals denaturation.

stem: In fractional distillation, the vapor at the top of the column is enriched in the:
explanation: Correct: C) Repeated condensation and vaporization concentrate the lower-boiling, more volatile component at the top. Why the others are wrong: A) Says the less volatile component, but it condenses lower in the column. B) A nonvolatile solute does not enter the vapor. D) Says the higher-boiling component, but it condenses and falls back down the column.
trap: Reversing enrichment so the higher-boiling component is assumed to collect at the column top.

stem: Why are boiling chips added to a liquid before distillation?

options.D: To promote smooth boiling and prevent bumping

explanation: Correct: D) Boiling chips provide nucleation sites for bubbles, promoting smooth boiling and preventing bumping. Why the others are wrong: A) They do not meaningfully change the boiling temperature. B) They are not drying agents and remove no water. C) They do not catalyze evaporation; they only supply nucleation sites.
trap: Thinking chips act as drying agents.

stem: In a simple distillation, where should the thermometer bulb be placed?

options.A: Just below the side arm leading to the condenser

explanation: Correct: A) The bulb just below the side arm measures the temperature of the vapor entering the condenser. Why the others are wrong: B) Placing it in the boiling liquid reads the liquid temperature, which exceeds the vapor temperature. C) Above the condenser is not in the vapor path at all. D) In the receiving flask it would read distillate temperature, not boiling vapor.
trap: Measuring liquid instead of vapor.

stem: Anhydrous magnesium sulfate is added to an organic layer to:
explanation: Correct: B) Anhydrous MgSO4 binds water as hydrates and is then filtered off, drying the organic layer. Why the others are wrong: A) It is not an acid-base reagent and does not neutralize acid. C) Extracting amines requires an acid wash, not a drying agent. D) It removes water; it does not change solvent polarity.
trap: Confusing drying with extraction.

stem: After extracting benzoate into aqueous NaOH, which step recovers benzoic acid?

options.C: Acidify with HCl to precipitate benzoic acid

explanation: Correct: C) Acidifying with HCl protonates benzoate, regenerating neutral, poorly water-soluble benzoic acid that precipitates. Why the others are wrong: A) More NaOH keeps it as benzoate in water. B) Evaporating ether does nothing since benzoate is in the aqueous layer. D) Brine would not protonate benzoate or precipitate the acid.
trap: Forgetting the neutralization.

stem: Why does HPLC require high pressure?

options.D: Small particles in the column create high resistance to flow

explanation: Correct: D) Small stationary-phase particles improve resolution but resist solvent flow, requiring high pressure. Why the others are wrong: A) HPLC uses a liquid mobile phase, so the sample is not a gas. B) Analytes in HPLC need not be volatile; that describes GC. C) Pressure only pushes solvent; separation arises from interactions with the stationary phase.
trap: Believing pressure itself separates compounds.

stem: In gel filtration, a small molecule elutes later than a large protein because:

options.A: It enters the pores and has a longer path

explanation: Correct: A) Small molecules enter the bead pores and take a longer path, so they elute later. Why the others are wrong: B) No covalent binding is involved in gel filtration. C) Charge is not the basis of separation in gel filtration. D) Hydrophobicity is not the basis of separation in gel filtration.
trap: Assuming binding explains retention.

stem: Adding beta-mercaptoethanol to a sample before SDS-PAGE allows resolution of:

options.B: Individual subunits linked by disulfide bonds

explanation: Correct: B) Beta-mercaptoethanol reduces disulfide bonds, so subunits linked by disulfides separate into individual chains on the gel. Why the others are wrong: A) SDS and reducing agent disrupt noncovalent complexes rather than preserving them. C) Native charge is masked by SDS. D) Oligomeric state in solution is lost by denaturation.
trap: Forgetting that SDS alone does not break disulfides.
